newsitem.title: RUSSIA: CIS states cautious on Russia-Belarus union.
newsitem.headline: CIS states cautious on Russia-Belarus union.

text.p: Russia and Belarus will cause a few nervous jitters in the former Soviet Union when they sign a charter on union on Friday, but most of their neighbours view the treaty with caution rather than outright concern.

Kazakhstan has been almost alone in continuing to voice its fears over the union, which it depicts as a threat to the future of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), the loose grouping of 12 former Soviet republics.
Other critics, such as Ukraine and Uzbekistan, have kept silent or softened their opposition as the treaty was diluted over the last few weeks until it became unlikely to have any practical impact.
"The union treaty is for the time being a more or less symbolic act," Russian political analyst Andrei Kortunov said.
But he said the union could still affect the CIS. "Moscow has decided to build relationships on a bilateral level rather than go through the multilateral channels of the CIS," he said.
That has irked Kazakhstan, which favours multinational agreements within the CIS rather than alliances between just two countries or small groups of states.

"It is impossible to unite socialism and the market economy," Interfax news agency quoted Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev as saying on Saturday in a comment on what some see as the incompatibility of Belarus' and Russia's economies.
Attacking Russia's minister for CIS affairs, he said: "Imperial ambitions which are popping out of some Russian politicians scare other countries away from Russia."

The CIS is divided into countries which favour rapid integration, those which want ties to develop more slowly, and others which tread extremely cautiously for fear that Moscow might gain domination over them again.
Beyond Kazakhstan, open criticism of union between Russia and Belarus is now hard to find among CIS leaders.

Uzbek President Islam Karimov cautioned against forcing "processes which have not matured" before Russia and Belarus signed an outline union agreement on April 2, but he has kept quiet on the union treaty since then.
Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma, whose country borders both Russia and Belarus, criticised the union treaty several weeks ago but has also modified his stance.
"This is the right of the Belarussian and Russian people to form some sort of union," Kuchma said on May 12, signing a border pact with Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko in Kiev.

Ukraine, the third Slav state in the CIS, has not responded to appeals for other countries to join the union. But it has cautiously tried to improve relations with Belarus, and Russian President Boris Yeltsin is due to visit Kiev next week.
Several CIS countries are taking a wait-and-see aproach.
"Any inter-state agreement will face the test of time. Time will prove all the advantages of the union or reveal its mistakes," Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan said last month.

Azerbaijan President Haydar Aliyev says his country has no intention of uniting with any other. His foreign policy adviser, Vafa Guluzade, called the union "an internal affair for Russia and Belarus".

Georgia said the union posed no danger for the CIS. "Georgia will be happy if the Russia-Belarus union works well for the people of both republics. I see nothing negative for integral processes in the CIS," presidential adviser Petre Mamradze said.
The Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, the only former Soviet republics not in the CIS, are being cautious.

"In practice...we cannot have anything against it," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Latvian Foreign Minister Valdis Birkavs as saying last month. "We are watching closely what has been happening and how it will affect earlier accords."
